steps.title: Open the CA list
steps.body: The Certification Authorities view lists every authority in this demo instance. Two independent scenarios are prepared: a standalone root CA and a two-level hierarchy.
steps.note: The CAs shown here were prepared before recording; the private keys never leave the KMS.

steps.title: Hierarchy overview
steps.body: The hierarchy view draws an arrow from each issuer to the CAs it signed. Demo-Root → Demo-Issuing is the chain of the second scenario, while Demo-Single sits alone as its own anchor.
steps.note: Arrows point from issuer to issued CA, matching the A → B notation used in the trust-model documentation.

steps.title: Standalone root CA
steps.body: Demo-Single is a self-signed root with no parent. It issues end-entity identities directly, with no intermediate level.
steps.note: A single-CA model keeps the chain depth at one; every identity can be validated against the root itself.

steps.title: Public CA certificate
steps.body: The Certificate PEM tab shows the public certificate of Demo-Single. This is the material a relying party would install as a trust anchor.
steps.note: Only the public certificate is shown; the signing key stays inside the KMS.

steps.title: Download the anchor
steps.body: Downloading the .pem file gives you the exact bytes to use as the CAfile in an external validator such as OpenSSL.
steps.note: The validation shown in this guide was run outside the recording: openssl verify returns OK for the identity against this anchor.

steps.title: Issued certificates
steps.body: The Certificates view lists every end-entity certificate. Both demo identities appear here with their issuing CA.
steps.note: Sample-data devices also appear in this table; the demo identities are the two Demo* entries.

steps.title: Single-scenario identity
steps.body: This identity was issued by Demo-Single. Its detail view shows the issuer, validity period and the two-certificate chain.
steps.note: The CSR was prepared before recording, so the private key was never exposed in the browser flow.

steps.title: Leaf certificate PEM
steps.body: The Certificate PEM tab shows the leaf certificate and the full chain, which for this scenario is just leaf plus root.
steps.note: The full-chain bundle already contains everything OpenSSL needs when the root is not installed locally.

steps.title: Download the identity
steps.body: Downloading the leaf certificate .pem completes the pair needed for external validation: identity plus anchor.
steps.note: openssl verify -CAfile demo-single.pem identity.pem returns OK for this certificate.

steps.title: Back to the CA list
steps.body: The second scenario uses a two-level hierarchy, so we return to Certification Authorities to inspect Demo-Root.
steps.note: The table view resets on navigation; the hierarchy radio is clicked again before opening the next CA.

steps.title: Hierarchy view again
steps.body: Switching back to the hierarchy view keeps the issuer-to-issued relationship visible while opening the root.
steps.note: This view is generated from the live CA inventory; it reflects the same data as the table.

steps.title: Hierarchy trust anchor
steps.body: Demo-Root is the self-signed anchor of the second scenario. It signs Demo-Issuing, which in turn issues end-entity identities.
steps.note: The intermediate CA has a shorter validity (5y) than the root (10y), so it expires first by design.

steps.title: Certificates again
steps.body: Back in the Certificates view, the hierarchy identity is listed with Demo-Issuing as its CA.
steps.note: The CA Issuer column here is the direct issuer, not the chain root.

steps.title: Hierarchy identity
steps.body: This identity was issued by Demo-Issuing, one level below the anchor. Its chain has three certificates: leaf, intermediate, root.
steps.note: This is the standard depth-2 hierarchy from RFC 5217 style deployments.

steps.title: Three-certifacte chain
steps.body: The Certificate PEM tab shows the leaf and a two-certificate full chain. The intermediate here is auxiliary material, not a trust anchor.
steps.note: Relying parties install only Demo-Root as anchor; the intermediate travels as untrusted input to the path builder.

steps.title: Download the hierarchy leaf
steps.body: Downloading this leaf .pem gives the third file of the hierarchy validation: leaf, intermediate, anchor.
steps.note: openssl verify -CAfile demo-root.pem -untrusted demo-issuing.pem identity.pem returns OK.

steps.title: Wrap up
steps.body: We return to the CA list to close with the hierarchy view, comparing both trust models side by side.
steps.note: The demo instance is disposable; none of this data is shared with a production environment.

steps.title: Both models at a glance
steps.body: Demo-Root → Demo-Issuing forms the hierarchy; Demo-Single is a separate anchor. A validator anchored in Demo-Single rejects the hierarchy identity, and vice versa.
steps.note: The wrong-anchor failure was verified outside the recording: OpenSSL reports 'unable to get local issuer certificate' when Demo-Single is used to validate the hierarchy identity.
